sentences.text: The genus contains a single species named Austroposeidon magnificus, which translates to "Magnificent Southern Poseidon." The name combines "austro" for South America and "Poseidon," the Greek god of earthquakes, while the species name refers to the large size of the known specimen.

Researchers established Austroposeidon as a new genus based on unique vertebral traits, including columnar laminae on the thirteenth cervical vertebra, split posterior laminae, curved first dorsal laminae, and forked frontmost laminae in dorsal vertebrae. These features, along with missing hyposphene-hypantrum articulations and camellate bone texture with air chambers, identify it as a titanosaur.
Austroposeidon is the largest dinosaur discovered in Brazil, with the single known adult specimen reaching about 25 meters in length.
CT scans revealed concentric alternating rings of camellate and dense tissue in the vertebrae, interpreted by researchers as growth rings.

The specimen was discovered in 1953 by Llewellyn Ivor Price in the Presidente Prudente Formation but was not formally described until 2016. Unfortunately, the original fossil site has been lost to urban development and could not be located by researchers.
A 2016 phylogenetic analysis recovered Austroposeidon as the sister taxon to the group Lognkosauria, though a 2022 study by Navarro et al. recovered it as a member of that same group.
Austroposeidon magnificus lived between 83.6 and 66 million years ago during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous in South America, spanning from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian.
